entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9022"/><div sID="gen15184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9022"/>3. He mentions his past religious consistency, not as a boast or a ground for justification; but according to the Old Testament dispensation, wherein temporal rewards (as long life, &c., <reference osisRef="Exod.20.12">Ex 20:12</reference>) followed legal obedience, he makes his religious conduct a plea for asking the prolongation of his life.<div eID="gen15184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked--</hi>Life is a journey; the pious "walk with God" (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.24">Ge 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.4">1Ki 9:4</reference>).<div eID="gen15185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect--</hi>sincere; not absolutely perfect, but aiming towards it (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mt 5:45</reference>); single-minded in walking as in the presence of God (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Ge 17:1</reference>). The letter of the Old Testament legal righteousness was, however, a standard very much below the spirit of the law as unfolded by Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.20-Matt.5.48">Mt 5:20-48</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2Co 3:6</reference>, 14, 17).<div eID="gen15186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wept sore--</hi>Josephus says, the reason why he wept so sorely was that being childless, he was leaving the kingdom without a successor. How often our wishes, when gratified, prove curses! Hezekiah lived to have a son; that son was the idolater Manasseh, the chief cause of God's wrath against Judah, and of the overthrow of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26">2Ki 23:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">27</reference>). <div eID="gen15187" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9027"/><div sID="gen15195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9027"/><hi type="bold">8. bring again--</hi>cause to return (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.12-Josh.10.14">Jos 10:12-14</reference>). In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9">2Ki 20:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.11">11</reference>, the choice is stated to have been given to Hezekiah, whether the shadow should go forward, or go back, ten degrees. Hezekiah replied, "It is a light thing (a less decisive miracle) for the shadow to go down (its usual direction) ten degrees: nay, but let it return backward ten degrees"; so Isaiah cried to Jehovah that it should be so, and it was so (compare <reference osisRef="Josh.10.12">Jos 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen15195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sundial of Ahaz--</hi>Herodotus (2.109) states that the sundial and the division of the day into twelve hours, were invented by the Babylonians; from them Ahaz borrowed the invention. He was one, from his connection with Tiglath-pileser, likely to have done so (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7">2Ki 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.10">10</reference>). "Shadow of the degrees" means the shadow made on the degrees. Josephus thinks these degrees were steps ascending to the palace of Ahaz; the time of day was indicated by the number of steps reached by the shadow. But probably a sundial, strictly so called, is meant; it was of such a size, and so placed, that Hezekiah, when convalescent, could witness the miracle from his chamber. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.38.21">Is 38:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">22</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9">2Ki 20:9</reference>, where translate, shall this shadow go forward, &c.; the dial was no doubt in sight, probably "in the middle court" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.4">2Ki 20:4</reference>), the point where Isaiah turned back to announce God's gracious answers to Hezekiah. Hence this particular sign was given. The retrogression of the shadow may have been effected by refraction; a cloud denser than the air interposing between the gnomon and dial would cause the phenomenon, which does not take from the miracle, for God gave him the choice whether the shadow should go forward or back, and regulated the time and place. Bosanquet makes the fourteenth year of Hezekiah to be 689 B.C., the known year of a solar eclipse, to which he ascribes the recession of the shadow. At all events, there is no need for supposing any revolution of the relative positions of the sun and earth, but merely an effect produced on the shadow (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9-2Kgs.20.11">2Ki 20:9-11</reference>); that effect was only local, and designed for the satisfaction of Hezekiah, for the Babylonian astronomers and king "sent to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2Ch 32:31</reference>), implying that it had not extended to their country. No mention of any instrument for marking time occurs before this dial of Ahaz, 700 B.C. The first mention of the "hour" is made by Daniel at Babylon (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Da 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen15196" type="x-p"/>
